intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, tell you what to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the examples in pencil before you read the steps, and answer the recall questions from memory.

sections.title: What EDA Is & Why
sections.big_idea: EDA is the open-minded first pass: **look, clean and question before you model**. It is the cheapest stage at which to be wrong.
in_plain_words: Exploratory data analysis describes, plots and questions a dataset to understand its shape, gaps and surprises. Tukey named it in 1977 and called it an attitude and a reliance on display. It asks what is in the file and what is wrong with it, while modelling asks whether X predicts Y.

Exploring and confirming are different logics. A pattern found by digging is a hypothesis to test on fresh data, and mixing the two silently is the commonest abuse. Skipped steps cost you a coding error modelled, a top-coded variable averaged or a subgroup that is mostly missing. Keep a log of what EDA caught.

diagram.caption: the order matters more than it sounds

key_terms.meaning: Open-minded first pass using summaries and pictures before testing.
Open-ended; generates questions; p-values mean little.
Pre-specified; tests a hypothesis, ideally on fresh data.
Tukey's term for plotting as central to analysis.
Written record of what exploration caught.

worked_example.title: Is this EDA or modelling?
worked_example.setup: Sort four questions between the two columns on slide 4.
steps: 'What is wrong with this file?' is an EDA question.
'Does X predict Y?' is a modelling question.
'Who is missing, and why?' is an EDA question.
'Controlling for what?' is a modelling question.
worked_example.answer: EDA, modelling, EDA, modelling; do the first and third before the others.

mistakes: Fitting a model to uninspected data, which runs and tells you nothing about the 30% of women with no income value.
Exploring until a pattern appears and then reporting it with a p-value as though it had been specified in advance.
Arriving with a story and noticing only the data that confirm it.

recall.q: Who named EDA and when?
recall.a: John W. Tukey, in 1977.

recall.q: What distinguishes exploratory from confirmatory work on hypotheses?
recall.a: Exploratory hypotheses are generated by the analysis; confirmatory ones are fixed before it.

recall.q: Name two things good EDA catches early.
recall.a: For example errors, gaps, shape, structure or surprises.

recall.q: What safeguard applies if you must do both on one dataset?
recall.a: Say which findings came from which.

recall.q: What are the four steps in order?
recall.a: Explore, describe, question, and only then model.

sections.title: Household Survey Data in India
sections.big_idea: Household surveys have **rosters, keys, frames and a design**. Know the unit, the survey's job and the universe before you compute.
in_plain_words: A household survey samples dwellings and records the household and each member. Households and members live in separate files joined on household ID plus person line, and the classic merge bug multiplies rows. People outside a sampled dwelling are out of frame, which the survey's silence will hide.

NSS, PLFS, NFHS and CMIE-CPHS answer different questions at different resolutions. PLFS is a new series that cannot be spliced onto earlier NSS rounds, and NFHS-5 fieldwork ran in two phases. Every statistic is per some unit with a denominator. The design is stratified, multistage and clustered, so check unit, key, weight, universe and missing codes on opening.

diagram.caption: match the survey to the question

key_terms.meaning: One row per household, keyed by household ID.
One row per person, keyed by household ID plus person line.
The entity each row represents.
Who was asked a given question at all.
The list of dwellings the sample is drawn from.
Primary sampling unit; a cluster such as a village.

worked_example.title: Count households and people
worked_example.setup: The slide's table has five rows: household 10231 with four members, and household 10232 with one.
steps: People: count rows. There are 4 + 1 = 5 persons.
Households: count distinct household IDs. There are 2.
Mean household size: collapse to household level first, then 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5.
A household-level toilet repeated on four member rows would count as four toilets at member level.

mistakes: Joining the rosters on household ID alone, which silently multiplies rows.
Splicing PLFS onto earlier NSS employment rounds to make one long trend.
Giving a district figure from an NSS round designed to state level.

recall.q: What key identifies a member row?
recall.a: Household ID plus person line number.

recall.q: What does PLFS give that NSS employment rounds did not?
recall.a: Annual rural and quarterly urban estimates since 2017-18.

recall.q: Why does NFHS-5 have a two-phase issue?
recall.a: Phase 1 finished before the pandemic and phase 2 largely after, with states unevenly split.

recall.q: What denominator belongs to the unemployment rate?
recall.a: The labour force.

recall.q: Name the five things to answer when a file opens.
recall.a: What one row is, the key, where the weight is, the universe, and which codes mean missing.

sections.title: The EDA Workflow
sections.big_idea: Six steps, **repeated**: load, inspect, clean, describe, visualise, question. The step people skip is the last, and clean steps live in a script.
in_plain_words: Load the data in the right format with IDs and codes as text and special missing codes preserved, and compare the row count with the documentation. Inspect every column for type, range, distinct values and missing counts. Clean in code, keeping the raw extract read-only.

Describe each variable with a summary that fits its type and report percent missing. Visualise because summaries hide shape, as Anscombe's quartet shows. Question by turning each pattern into a written question. The loop repeats: a plot sends you back to cleaning and a question sends you back to the codebook.

key_terms.meaning: The original file, kept read-only and dated.
Digits like 0457 lost if IDs are read as numbers.
Rule making a question blank for some respondents.
Four datasets with identical statistics and different shapes.
Dated list of questions EDA raised.

worked_example.title: Check the load
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. The survey report documents 10,000 households and your file has 5,000 rows.
steps: Compare the counts: 5,000 ÷ 10,000 = 50%.
Half the documented sample is suspicious; the slide lists 'only the first file loaded' with no error.
Check IDs: a household ID such as 0457 becoming 457 would break merges silently.
Fix the load before any other work.
worked_example.answer: Half the sample is missing; load every file with IDs read as text.

mistakes: Hand-editing the raw file instead of writing every change in code.
Reading ID and code columns as numbers, so leading zeros vanish.
Ending EDA with a folder of plots and no written questions.

recall.q: Why keep the raw extract read-only?
recall.a: So that when a number changes you can re-run from an unaltered source.

recall.q: What is the first check after loading?
recall.a: Compare the row count with the survey report.

recall.q: What is the warning when a skip-pattern question has zero missing?
recall.a: The not-applicable code was probably read as a real value.

recall.q: What should you report next to every statistic?
recall.a: Percent missing.

recall.q: Which step ends EDA usefully?
recall.a: Question, with the open questions written down.

sections.title: Knowing Your Variables
sections.big_idea: The codebook is your map. **Level of measurement decides which statistics are legal**, and a code is a label until the dictionary says otherwise.
in_plain_words: A data dictionary defines every variable: its meaning, units, allowed values, codes, special missing codes and who it applies to. Universe explains most missing data, and reference period is often decisive. Four levels of measurement, nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio, control the maths you may use.

Coded numbers such as state codes are labels with no quantity behind them, and a mean of them prints like any other mean. Convert coded columns to labelled factors early. Special codes like 99 must be recoded to missing. Derived variables embed judgements, so document them, and keep a profile of each variable as a script-generated table.

levels.label: Ratio
levels.sub: equal gaps, true zero; all maths

diagram.caption: the more structure, the more maths is legal

key_terms.meaning: Document defining each variable, its codes and universe.
The time window a question covers, such as last 7 days.
Labels with no order, such as religion.
Ordered with unequal gaps, such as wealth quintile.
A variable you build, such as MPCE.
One-line summary of a variable's meaning, type and gaps.

worked_example.title: Which summary is legal?
worked_example.setup: Pair four survey variables with the valid maths from the levels table.
steps: Religion code is nominal: counts and the mode.
Wealth quintile is ordinal: median and rank.
Year of birth is interval: mean and difference.
Consumption is ratio: all maths, including ratios.
worked_example.answer: Counts, median, mean and difference, and all maths, in that order.

mistakes: Averaging state codes or caste category codes.
Reporting a 'mean quintile of 3.2', which assumes equal gaps between quintiles.
Skipping the reference period, so last week and last year are treated as the same measure.

recall.q: What does universe tell you?
recall.a: Who was supposed to answer the question, which explains by-design missing data.

recall.q: Which field is most often skipped and most often decisive?
recall.a: Reference period.

recall.q: What is the halfway test?
recall.a: Whether the point halfway between two values means something.

recall.q: What should you do with 99 or 999 codes?
recall.a: Recode them to explicit missing before any summary.

recall.q: Why generate the variable profile in the script?
recall.a: So it regenerates when the data change instead of going stale.

sections.title: Univariate Exploration
sections.big_idea: Look at **one variable at a time**. Choose the first look by type, read the shape, and report the centre that suits it.
in_plain_words: Univariate work finds most problems. Run a frequency table for categorical variables, with n and %, and a histogram plus five-number summary for continuous ones. Check dates against fieldwork and IDs for duplicates. Read shape: centre, spread, skew, modes, gaps and spikes, trying a few bin widths.

Skewed money variables need the median, and the mean is pulled up by the tail. Right-skewed is the common case in development data, and a bimodal variable needs splitting into groups. Density plots compare groups but smoothing is a choice. A log scale is an exploratory lens, with zeros as its obstacle.

left.title: Right-skewed (typical)
items: Report the median, say it is skewed

right.title: Roughly symmetric
items: Either is fine; mean with SD

diagram.caption: shape decides the centre to report

key_terms.meaning: Count and percentage of every level.
Bars of counts across bins; shows skew and gaps.
Min, Q1, median, Q3, max.
Q3 minus Q1, the spread of the middle 50%.
Two peaks, often two populations pooled.
Axis spreading low values and pulling in a long tail.

worked_example.title: Measure the skew
worked_example.setup: Use the slide's diagnostic on MPCE with mean 3,240 and median 2,700, both from the telling-the-story slide.
steps: Mean minus median: 3,240 − 2,700 = 540.
As a fraction of the median: 540 ÷ 2,700 = 20%.
For Indian consumption data a gap of 15-25% is ordinary, so 20% sits inside it.
Report the median, and say the variable is right-skewed.
worked_example.answer: A 20% gap, ordinary for consumption; report the median.

mistakes: Reporting a median with a standard deviation, a sign the summary was assembled.
Calling a distribution bimodal on a single histogram without trying other bin widths.
Using a log scale with zeros without stating how the zeros were handled.

recall.q: What should a frequency table show?
recall.a: Both n and %.

recall.q: Which centre for skewed money?
recall.a: The median.

recall.q: Why plot both histogram and density?
recall.a: The histogram shows what is there; the density shows how groups compare.

recall.q: What problem does log(0) cause?
recall.a: It is undefined, so the usual fixes change the plot and must be stated.

recall.q: Why look at min and max every time?
recall.a: Impossible values live there.

sections.title: Spotting Trouble
sections.big_idea: Six detectors run on every column. **Ask why a value is missing**, flag outliers instead of deleting them, and test rules for logical contradictions.
in_plain_words: The watchlist covers missing values, impossible values, special codes, top-coding, heaping and duplicates. Each has a one-line detector. Missingness has mechanisms: by design, completely at random, at random given observed variables, and not at random, which biases results you cannot repair from the data.

Cross-tabulate missingness against sector, sex, state, wealth and interviewer, and treat a missing flag as an outcome. Outliers may be errors or the story, so report estimates both ways. Rules flag candidates, logic assertions run in the cleaning script, and top-coding biases the mean and inequality measures downward.

diagram.root: What can be wrong with a column
diagram.caption: detectors by kind of problem

key_terms.meaning: Values bunched at round numbers such as ages 0, 5, 10.
Capping a variable at a maximum.
Gaps explained by variables you can observe.
Gaps depending on the missing value itself.
Member row whose household row was lost.
Flag beyond Q1 − 1.5×IQR or Q3 + 1.5×IQR.

worked_example.title: Apply the IQR rule
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A variable has Q1 = 40 and Q3 = 100.
steps: Fence width: 1.5 × 60 = 90.
Upper fence: 100 + 90 = 190.
Lower fence: 40 − 90 = −50, so nothing below is flagged for a non-negative variable.
Treat values above 190 as candidates for review and never as automatic deletions.
worked_example.answer: Values above 190 are candidates; a human decides.

mistakes: Silently dropping outliers, which can delete a real district.
Applying the IQR rule to skewed consumption and reading the flagged tail as a data-quality problem.
Using complete-case analysis when richer households refuse income, which hides downward bias.

recall.q: What does the cheapest detector for duplicates compare?
recall.a: Count of rows against count of distinct keys.

recall.q: What does a wall of cases at one value suggest?
recall.a: Top-coding.

recall.q: Which missingness mechanism can bias results you cannot remove?
recall.a: Missing not at random.

recall.q: What bias do top-coded incomes cause?
recall.a: The mean and inequality measures are biased downward.

recall.q: What is the honest procedure for a real extreme value?
recall.a: Report the estimate with and without it.

sections.title: Bivariate & Multivariate Exploration
sections.big_idea: Look at variables together, and **add the third variable early**. Show counts, choose percentage direction deliberately and disaggregate before concluding.
in_plain_words: Pick the tool by the pair: cross-tabs for two categories, grouped medians and box plots for a category and a number, scatter for two numbers, and faceting for any pair by a third. Row and column percentages answer different questions, and counts should sit beside percentages. Suppress cells below a threshold.

Correlation captures straight lines only and is moved by outliers, so plot beside it and prefer Spearman for skewed money. A heatmap maps questions and finds near-duplicates. Simpson's paradox and ecological fallacy mean aggregates mislead, so split by sector, state, wealth, sex and social group before concluding.

key_terms.meaning: A table of two categorical variables.
Percent within each row group.
Rank correlation, less swayed by large values.
Aggregate trend reversing within subgroups.
Reading a group-level pattern as an individual truth.
A group difference that reflects a difference in mix.

worked_example.title: Read the toilet cross-tab
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. Rural: 5,180 with a toilet and 2,020 without. Urban: 2,610 with and 190 without. All: 7,790 with a toilet.
steps: Rural households: 5,180 + 2,020 = 7,200.
Rural row percentage: 5,180 ÷ 7,200 = 72%.
Urban households: 2,610 + 190 = 2,800.
Urban row percentage: 2,610 ÷ 2,800 = 93.2%.
Column question, share of toilet households that are urban: 2,610 ÷ 7,790 = 33.5%.
worked_example.answer: 72% rural and 93.2% urban have a toilet; a third of households with toilets are urban.

mistakes: Showing percentages without counts, so a figure built on 190 households looks like one on 19,000.
Choosing the wrong percentage direction and answering a different question.
Reporting an aggregate difference without checking it inside the obvious subgroups.

recall.q: Which direction answers 'of rural households, what share have a toilet'?
recall.a: Row percentage with sector in rows.

recall.q: What threshold convention does the slide mention for suppression?
recall.a: 25 unweighted cases.

recall.q: Why prefer Spearman for skewed money?
recall.a: A handful of very large values cannot set the answer.

recall.q: How many correlations in a 20-variable heatmap?
What does a correlation of 0.99 between columns usually mean?
recall.a: One column was derived from the other.

sections.title: Survey Weights & Design Effects in EDA
sections.big_idea: Unweighted exploration describes the sample. **Weight any number that describes the population** and report what the design does to precision.
in_plain_words: Household surveys over-sample small groups and adjust for non-response, so the raw file is not a miniature India. A weight says how many people a row represents. Different files carry different weights, and the wrong one is silent. Label every table weighted or unweighted.

Clustering and weighting inflate variance, which the design effect measures. DEFF = 2 halves the effective sample, and it belongs to each estimate. Use survey-aware tools, declare stratum, PSU and weight once, and check the unweighted count behind every estimate. A survey is reliable only down to the level it was designed for.

diagram.note: 10,000 rows with DEFF = 2 carry the information of about 5,000

key_terms.meaning: How many people a record stands for in the population.
Deliberately interviewing more of a small group.
Variance inflation versus a simple random sample.
Nominal n divided by DEFF.
Strata split the frame; PSUs are the clusters sampled.
The geography a survey is reliable for.

worked_example.title: Effective sample size
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A survey has n = 10,000. Typical DEFF for a clustered household survey runs 1.5-2.5.
steps: At the high end: 10,000 ÷ 2.5 = 4,000.
Intervals that ignore DEFF are too narrow by this loss.
worked_example.answer: Between about 4,000 and 6,667 effective households, with 5,000 at DEFF = 2.

mistakes: Publishing unweighted figures without saying so, so a sample description is read as a national estimate.
Using household weights for a person-level rate.
Drilling NFHS to a cell with 11 households and reporting a precise percentage.

recall.q: What does an over-sampled high-rate state do to the unweighted national figure?
recall.a: It inflates it.

recall.q: How do you check you chose the right weight?
recall.a: Reproduce one of the survey report's published figures.

recall.q: Which Stata command declares the design?
recall.a: svyset.

recall.q: Is DEFF a property of the survey or the estimate?
recall.a: Of each estimate.

recall.q: What does the slide say beats assuming DEFF = 1 silently?
recall.a: An assumed DEFF stated openly.

sections.title: Visual EDA Done Well
sections.big_idea: Plot every continuous variable once. **Use shared scales, honest baselines and counts** so that a plot reveals shape without misleading its author.
in_plain_words: Plotting is the heart of EDA because the eye catches skew, two populations, curved relations and spikes at codes. Small multiples and faceting disaggregate visually, but need shared scales and enough cases per panel. Box plots compare distributions and hide bimodality and counts.

Honest axes start bar charts at zero, because truncation makes a 4-point rise look like a leap. Large surveys overplot, so use transparency, sampling, binning or contours and accept trade-offs. A checklist covers chart type, baseline, labels, log scale, weighting, disaggregation and n. Subtitle unweighted plots.

key_terms.meaning: Many identical small charts in a grid.
Splitting one plot into panels by a category.
Quartiles, median and outliers drawn per group.
Points piling into a blob that hides density.
Two-dimensional binning of dense points.
A bar axis that starts at zero.

worked_example.title: Why truncation misleads
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. Coverage rises from 90 to 94, as in the slide's two charts.
steps: True rise: 94 − 90 = 4 points.
Ratio of the two bars on a zero baseline: 94 ÷ 90 = 1.04.
With the axis starting at 90, the first bar has height 0 and the second 4, so the rise looks enormous.
Start the bar axis at zero and label the units.
worked_example.answer: Same 4-point rise; only the zero baseline shows it as about 4%.

mistakes: Auto-scaling each panel in a grid, which turns it into separate charts that only look adjacent.
Faceting a 10,000-household survey by district, which leaves too few cases per panel.
Leaving an unweighted plot unlabelled, so a sample picture is read as a national one.

recall.q: Why order small-multiple panels?
recall.a: Ordering is free and does much of the analytical work.

recall.q: What do box plots hide?
recall.a: Bimodality and the number of observations.

recall.q: Name two fixes for overplotting.
recall.a: Transparency, smaller points, sampling, 2-D binning or contours.

recall.q: Where should 'unweighted sample' appear?
recall.a: In the subtitle, since subtitles travel with screenshots.

recall.q: How many panels suit small multiples?
recall.a: About 4-30.

sections.title: From EDA to Questions & Hypotheses
sections.big_idea: EDA ends where testing begins. **A found pattern is a hypothesis**, and every finding travels with its unit, weights, level and caveats.
in_plain_words: Exploration is generative and its findings are hypotheses. The clean version is to split the data, explore one half and test on the other. EDA can describe samples, reveal quality problems, compare groups with weights, suggest relationships and sharpen questions. It cannot prove cause, confirm what it found or establish significance by eye.

Forking paths make noise look real: twenty slices give a 64% chance of a striking result by luck. Be honest about how much you explored. Record unit, weights, level, caveats and explored-or-tested status with every finding, in the same file as the number, and translate findings into plain language.

diagram.caption: the hand-off from exploration to testing

key_terms.meaning: A precise claim stated before testing.
Many possible analyses, so some pattern appears by chance.
Exploring until something looks significant and reporting it.
Data kept back to test what exploration suggested.
Writing down what you will test beforehand.

worked_example.title: Count your slices
worked_example.setup: Use the slide's table of slices tried against the chance of one striking result.
steps: 1 slice: about 5% at the usual threshold.
5 slices: about 23%.
20 slices: about 64%, a modest afternoon's work.
50 slices: about 92%.
So a surprising subgroup result found on the twentieth cut deserves scepticism.
worked_example.answer: The chance climbs steeply; say how many slices you tried.

mistakes: Reporting a subgroup pattern found on the twentieth cut as a headline.
Omitting the unit, weights or caveats, so the number arrives stripped of what qualifies it.
Using 'significant' for a pattern that came from the data itself.

recall.q: What is the cleanest way to test an explored pattern?
recall.a: Split the data: explore one half, test on the other.

recall.q: Name two things EDA can legitimately conclude.
recall.a: For example describe the sample, reveal data-quality problems, or suggest relationships worth testing.

recall.q: What are the five lines to record with a finding?
recall.a: Unit and denominator, weighted or not, level it holds at, data-quality caveats, explored or tested.

recall.q: What is the procedural defence against p-hacking?
recall.a: Write down in advance what you will test, log what you looked at, and report the search.

recall.q: How would you phrase 'DEFF = 2' for a decision maker?
recall.a: This sample is about as informative as 5,000 independent households.

sections.title: Tools & Reproducibility
sections.big_idea: Choose tools that **understand weights**, keep scripts from raw extract to result, and record sources, versions and seeds so the work can be re-run.
in_plain_words: R with srvyr, Python with samplics, Stata with svyset and SPSS Complex Samples handle survey design, and spreadsheets do not. Spreadsheets are fine for a first look, and their failure mode is no record of what was changed. Choose what your team can maintain.

A documented script from raw extract to result answers a reviewer's questions directly. Keep the raw extract read-only and dated, separate cleaning from analysis, name files by version and date, and record source, download date and filters. Download the codebook beside the data, and note the exact file version.

left.title: Fragile
items: Nobody can reproduce it next month

right.title: Reliable
items: Re-run, audit, hand to a colleague

diagram.caption: the golden rule: never edit the raw file

key_terms.meaning: Code from raw extract to result that can be re-run.
A fixed starting value for anything random.
Software that handles weights, strata and clusters.
Source of unit-level survey files, such as microdata.gov.in.
Source, date and exact file name of the data used.

worked_example.title: What does the script answer?
worked_example.setup: Pair four reviewer questions with the script's answer from the reproducibility slide.
steps: 'Where did this number come from?' A line in a file.
'What did you exclude?' The filter, with its reason.
'Can you redo it for 2019?' Change one path.
'Why did this change?' The diff.
worked_example.answer: A line, a filter with a reason, one path, and a diff.

mistakes: Naming files final_FINAL_v3 instead of using versions and dates.
Leaving the codebook on a portal that later reorganises.
Choosing the most powerful tool when nobody on the team can maintain the script.

recall.q: Which tools have built-in survey design support?
recall.a: Stata with svyset, R with srvyr and survey, SPSS Complex Samples, and Python partly via samplics.

recall.q: Why keep the raw extract read-only and dated?
recall.a: So every cleaning step lives in code and can be audited.

recall.q: What two one-line habits make 're-run it' real?
recall.a: Set a seed and record package versions.

recall.q: Which portal gives NSS and PLFS unit-level data?
recall.a: microdata.gov.in, with registration.

recall.q: What does census data give you?
recall.a: Tables only, with no microdata.

notes.2: Use the agenda to see where the course goes: what EDA is, the surveys you will meet, the workflow, variables, one-variable views, trouble-spotting, relationships, weights, plots, hypotheses and tools. **Sections 2 and 8 are specific to household surveys**, so read them even if you know EDA from another setting.
notes.4: Think of EDA as detective work done before any model. Use the two-column table to keep the questions straight: EDA asks what is in the file, what is wrong with it and who is missing. **The order matters**, because a model will run on uninspected data and say nothing about the missing 30% of women.
notes.5: Tukey named EDA in 1977, and his quotation matters: it is **an attitude and a reliance on display**, so it cannot be completed like a checklist. Use the table to remember what he changed: exploration became a legitimate stage, plotting became central, and median and IQR serve messy data.
notes.6: Keep the two modes apart. Exploratory work generates hypotheses and p-values mean little, while confirmatory work fixes the hypothesis first. **Never explore until a pattern appears and then report it with a p-value** as if specified in advance. If you do both on one dataset, say which findings came from which.
notes.7: Hold your story loosely. The table gives four stories and what EDA might find behind each, such as a mean that rose while the median did not. **None of these says the story is wrong**; each says the data cannot yet carry it. Write down the story you arrived with, then test it against these.
notes.8: Learn the four-step order: explore, describe, question, and only then model. The table shows what ships when a step is skipped, such as age 999 in the mean. **Nothing errors**, and the output looks correct, so make the steps a habit and not a reaction to a warning.
notes.9: Use this list as your reason to budget time for EDA: errors, gaps, shape, structure and surprises. The table prices each miss, for example confidence intervals far too narrow when clustering and weights are ignored. **Keep a written log of what EDA caught**; it is your evidence of data quality when a reviewer asks.
notes.10: The roadmap runs from foundations to practice. Notice the closing line: the data you meet is patterned on NSS, PLFS and NFHS. **Keep one of those surveys in mind** as you read, so every example attaches to a file you might open at work.
notes.12: A household survey samples dwellings and then asks about the household and each member. The table lists design choices that limit what you can say. The quiet one is the frame: **people outside a sampled dwelling are invisible**, and the survey's silence about them looks identical to their absence. State the exclusion explicitly.
notes.13: Know the two rosters: one row per household, one row per person. Merge them on the right key, household ID plus person line. The classic bug is **joining on household ID alone**, which silently multiplies rows. Check the row count before and after every merge, and ask why a join that grows your data grew.
notes.14: Count by the right unit. Four rows can be one household, so count distinct household IDs for households and rows for people. The warning at the foot is vivid: **five members in a household with a toilet become five toilets** at member level. Put the unit in every table, as in 'Unit: households (n = 8,140)'.
notes.15: Learn each survey by name and job. Choose by unit and resolution, since NFHS gives district estimates and NSS consumption is designed to state level, so a **district figure from NSS has false precision**. When two sources disagree, check reference period, universe and question wording before suspecting error.
notes.16: PLFS replaced the NSS employment series from 2017-18, with a new design, questionnaire and sampling. It is a different series, so **splicing it onto earlier rounds is a well-known error**. If you need a long trend, present two series and say why, because a single line implies continuity that does not exist.
notes.17: NFHS is India's DHS, with district estimates and biomarkers, and the slide gives the latest round as NFHS-6 (2023–24), fact sheets released in May 2026. Remember what it lacks: consumption, income and a panel. For NFHS-5, **the two-phase fieldwork is a real confounder**, since states are not evenly split between phases.
notes.18: Treat CMIE-CPHS as a complement to the official surveys: timely and a true panel, but not an official product, with attrition and a sampling frame criticised for under-covering the poorest. Trust its trends more than its levels. For EDA the practical point is that **if you cannot share the data, a reader cannot check you**.
notes.19: Decide the unit and the denominator before computing. The table pairs each statistic with its unit and its denominator, such as women tested for anaemia. **Most misquoted statistics are denominator errors**; the unemployment rate falls when people stop looking for work. Put the denominator in the variable name.
notes.20: Survey design explains why plain sample statistics mislead: stratified, multistage and clustered. Clustering surprises people, because households in one village resemble each other and **each adds less information** than an independent draw. For exploration, unweighted plots find errors but misdescribe the population, so know which you are doing.
notes.21: Answer the five questions in writing at the top of your script: what is one row, what is the key, where is the weight, what is the universe, which codes mean missing. It takes ten minutes and is the **highest-return habit** in the course. A question you cannot answer from the documentation is itself a finding.
notes.23: Run the loop of six steps: load, inspect, clean, describe, visualise, question. Expect to go round it many times, and use the 'done when' column to know when a step is finished. **The step people skip is the last one**, without which EDA ends in a folder of plots nobody can act on.
notes.24: Load carefully, because errors here are silent. Read ID and code columns as text, or a household ID like 0457 becomes 457 and merges fail without an error. Keep special missing codes, and **check the loaded row count against the survey report** before anything else. It is one line of code.
notes.25: Inspect every column, including those you never plan to use. The red flags column tells you what to look for: suspiciously round row counts, numbers stored as text, impossible min and max, few distinct values. **Zero missing where a skip pattern exists** is a stronger warning than a high missing count.
notes.26: Clean in a script and never in the raw file. Use the table as a swap list: flag instead of deleting, create a new variable instead of overwriting, comment the reason for each recode. **A cleaning script that runs from raw extract to analysis table** is the only honest answer to 'can you reproduce this?'
notes.27: Describe every variable with the summary that suits its type, and report percent missing next to every statistic. A mean over 60% of the sample is a different object from a mean over 99%. Describing the variables you will not use is where **codebook errors surface**.
notes.28: Always plot after describing. Summaries can hide bimodality, curved relationships, spikes at top-codes and heaping, as the left column shows. Anscombe's quartet is the classic demonstration. In exploration, **a plot need not be presentable**: draw it fast, look, and throw it away.
notes.29: End every pass with written questions: the table turns patterns into questions, such as 'is one variable derived from another?' Those questions become your analysis plan. **Write them in the script, dated**, so you can later separate what EDA suggested from what a test confirmed.
notes.31: Download the codebook with the data and keep both in the same folder. Without it, a '2' could mean female, urban, no or missing, and **no inspection recovers the meaning**. The table shows what you cannot do without it: compute a mean safely, state a denominator, compare surveys or choose a weight.
notes.32: Read the codebook before you look at the data. Universe explains most 'missing' data, since a pregnancy question is blank for men by design. **Reference period is the field most often skipped and most often decisive**, because last week and last year give different employment rates. Say which you used in the sentence reporting the number.
notes.33: The level of measurement decides which statistics are legal. You can average ratio data such as age, but not nominal codes, and a wealth quintile is a rank. **Report the median, mode and full distribution for ordinal data** and avoid a 'mean quintile of 3.2' that assumes equal gaps.
notes.34: Sort variables into categories and measures, and check the codebook and not the column type. Education stored as 1–8 looks numeric but its mean is meaningless. Use the halfway test: **does the point halfway between two values mean something?** Between 4 and 6 years of schooling it does; between 'primary' and 'higher secondary' it does not.
notes.35: Survey files store almost everything as numbers, so a column's type tells you little. State = 9 means Uttar Pradesh and is no quantity. A mean state code of 14.7 **prints exactly like a mean age**. Convert coded columns to labelled factors first, after which the software refuses to average them.
notes.36: Recode special codes to missing before any summary, and keep 'not applicable' apart from 'not stated'. The first is design and shrinks the denominator; the second is non-response. A histogram finds these fastest: **a lone spike at 99** in a variable that otherwise stops at 60 is unmistakable.
notes.37: Every derived variable embeds a judgement, such as which items count in MPCE or which line defines poverty. Derive in a script, check the new distribution, and **write the definition as a comment** in words a colleague could apply independently. Otherwise 'poor' becomes a column whose reasoning nobody recalls.
notes.38: Build a one-line profile for each variable: meaning, type, range and codes, universe, percent missing. Keep it as a table generated by the script. The reason is stated at the foot: **a profile updated by hand will be wrong within a month**, while a generated one refreshes when the data change.
notes.40: Start with one variable at a time and use the table to choose the first look by type. Do it for all variables before bivariate work, since a relationship between two badly coded variables is not worth exploring. **Nearly every error in a published table** would have been visible in a plain frequency table.
notes.41: Run a frequency table for every categorical variable. Read it for tiny levels, impossible levels and the size of 'not stated'. Percentages need a stated base: here 1.0% is not stated, so a coverage figure over all rows differs slightly from one over stated answers. **Report both n and %** so the table can be checked and pooled.
notes.42: Read the long right tail first: consumption, like income and landholding, is right-skewed, so a few households spend many times the typical amount. This is why the mean misleads. The chart is illustrative, patterned on NSS consumption. **Draw this histogram yourself on your data** before you choose a summary.
notes.43: Use the list of features as a reading routine: centre, spread, skew, modes, gaps and spikes. The table maps each oddity to a cause, such as two peaks meaning two populations pooled. **Try two or three bin widths** before deciding a distribution is bimodal, since one histogram can manufacture or hide a peak.
notes.44: Use density plots to compare shapes, such as rural against urban consumption, and keep the histogram alongside. Smoothing is a choice, and density estimates of non-negative variables can draw a tail below zero. For EDA, **plot both**: the histogram shows what is there, the density shows how groups compare.
notes.45: Report mean with SD and median with IQR, since a median with an SD is a tell that the summary was assembled. Use the five-number summary when the shape is unknown. **Look at min and max every single time**, because impossible values live there, even if you seldom report them.
notes.46: For skewed money, trust the median. In the illustrative chart the mean sits well above the median because a long tail of high spenders drags it up. For consumption, income and land, **report the median** and say the variable is skewed so the reader knows why the mean is absent.
notes.47: Name the skew and choose accordingly. Right-skewed means mean above median, so use the median. The bimodal row matters most and is least acted on: **no single number describes two peaks**, so split the groups. A gap of mean minus median over the median of 15-25% is ordinary for Indian consumption.
notes.48: A log scale is an exploratory lens for strongly right-skewed money. Label the axis as logged and back-transform before reporting rupee figures. Zeros are the practical obstacle, since log(0) is undefined and both common fixes change the plot. **State the fix** and remember that readers may read a log axis as linear.
notes.50: Use the watchlist as six detectors that run on every column: missing values, impossible values, special codes, top-coding, heaping and duplicates. Each is one line of code. **Run them automatically as part of loading**, because automation stops them being skipped on the day you are in a hurry.
notes.51: A missingness bar chart across variables is one of the most useful EDA plots. This one is illustrative, but the lesson holds: income and 'not applicable' fields are usually the worst, and that is rarely random. **Draw one before any analysis** and let it direct your questions.
notes.52: Ask why a value is missing, because the answer decides what helps. Skip patterns shrink the denominator, 'at random' means explained by variables you can see, and 'not at random' biases results in ways you cannot remove. The richest refusing income **biases inequality measures downward**; complete-case analysis hides it.
notes.53: Cross-tabulate missingness against sector, sex, state, wealth and interviewer or PSU. Create a missing flag and treat it as an outcome. The last row is forgotten most: **missingness clustered in a few PSUs is a fieldwork artefact**, visible in about four lines of code. Patterned gaps are often the most interesting thing in the file.
notes.54: Never silently drop outliers: flag, explain, decide, and log. Check whether the value is possible, whether it is a code, whether it is one record or many, and whether it changes the conclusion. **Report the estimate both ways** for a real extreme value. The district with triple the stunting rate may be the story.
notes.55: Use rules to flag candidates and let a human decide. The table shows where each rule fails: the IQR rule flags a whole skewed tail, and the SD rule suits normal data. **Automating the decision is how a real district gets deleted for being poor.** Combine range, logic and visual checks.
notes.56: Write the logic the data must obey as a list of assertions your cleaning script runs and reports on, then re-run on every extract. The list grows each time someone finds a new way for data to be wrong. The cross-file rule catches **orphaned records**, member rows whose household was dropped upstream.
notes.57: Top-coding caps a variable at a ceiling, so look for a wall of cases at one value by tabulating the maximum. It makes the mean and upper tail unreliable and **biases the mean and inequality measures downward**. The median is usually unaffected, which is another reason to prefer it here.
notes.58: Read the before and after as proof of why cleaning matters. The impossible sliver above 110 disappears after recoding to missing. It is small in count, but it would have distorted any mean age and **revealed a data-entry problem worth reporting**. The chart is illustrative.
notes.60: Move from one variable to two or three with the matching tool: cross-tab, grouped summaries, scatter, correlation matrix and faceting. **Add the third variable early**, because most apparent bivariate relationships change when you split by sector, state or wealth. Watch for composition effects, where a group difference is really an age or urban mix.
notes.61: Read the toilet cross-tab with row percentages: 71.9% of rural households have a toilet against 93.2% of urban. Show counts beside percentages, because a cell of 93.2% built on 190 households looks the same as one built on 19,000. **Flag cells below a threshold** such as 25 unweighted cases.
notes.62: Choose the percentage direction by the sentence you want to write. Row percentages answer 'of rural households, what share have a toilet', and column percentages answer a different question. **The direction encodes a causal reading**, so put the grouping variable in rows and read your sentence aloud to check it.
notes.63: Grouping a continuous variable by a category is the commonest development EDA move. Here median consumption is shown by social group, patterned on NSS and illustrative. Use the median for skewed money, and **print the group n** so a reader can judge the precision of each bar.
notes.64: Compare spread as well as centre. Plotting quartiles by sector shows urban consumption is both higher and more spread out, a fact medians alone would hide. A true box plot is awkward in this toolkit, so the **quartile chart is a fair substitute** for exploration. The data are illustrative.
notes.65: A clear negative pattern appears between female literacy and total fertility rate across states. Remember it is a state-level picture. **Avoid reading it as an individual truth**: the next slides on correlation and disaggregation explain why. The chart is illustrative, patterned on Census 2011 and NFHS-5.
notes.66: Plot before you quote r. Correlation summarises straight-line association only, says nothing of slope or cause, and is moved by single outliers. Two datasets can share r = 0.8 and look different. **For skewed money, Spearman is the more honest summary**, because a handful of large values cannot set it.
notes.67: Use the heatmap as a map of questions. A strong cell says look here, then you plot the pair. With 20 variables there are 190 correlations, so some will be large by chance. **Its most reliable use is spotting near-duplicates**: a correlation of 0.99 usually means one column was derived from the other.
notes.68: Disaggregate before concluding, by sector, state, wealth, sex and social group. Simpson's paradox appears whenever group sizes differ and outcomes vary by group, which describes most state comparisons in India. **If a difference holds in every subgroup**, say so, because that is a stronger claim than the aggregate.
notes.70: Weights separate describing the sample from estimating the population. Unweighted figures are fine for finding errors and legitimate to publish when labelled. **Label every table weighted or unweighted**: one word turns a mistake into a caveat and stops a sample description being read as a national estimate.
notes.71: A survey weight says how many people or households a record stands for. Different files use different weights: household, person, woman, child. **Using the wrong weight is silent** and gives a plausible number. If unsure, reproduce one of the survey report's published figures to confirm your choice.
notes.72: Surveys over-sample small groups on purpose so they have usable estimates, then weights restore national balance. The consequence is that the raw file is no miniature India. **Any raw share of states, sectors or groups is wrong in a knowable direction**, so check the design before looking at shares.
notes.73: Compare the weighted and unweighted bars in the illustrative chart. State estimates match, but the unweighted national figure is inflated by an over-sampled high-rate state, producing about a four-point swing. **The headline number changes** when you weight, which is why this section exists.
notes.74: Design effect measures how much clustering and weighting inflate variance compared with a simple random sample. DEFF = 2 halves the effective sample. It belongs to each estimate and the survey as a whole has no single value, with geographic variables clustering most. **An assumed DEFF stated openly beats silently assuming 1.**
notes.75: Divide nominal n by DEFF to get the effective sample: 10,000 with DEFF = 2 carries the information of about 5,000. Ignore it and your **confidence intervals will be too narrow**, claiming more precision than the data support. Keep the calculation in your notes next to the estimate.
notes.76: Declare stratum, PSU and weight once at the top of your script, then let a survey-aware tool handle every estimate. Applying weights to the point estimate alone gets the number right and the **uncertainty wrong**. Report whether each figure is weighted and at what level it holds.
notes.77: Respect the resolution at which the survey was designed. Drilling to a tiny subgroup until a cell holds 11 households yields precise-looking noise. **Check the unweighted count behind every estimate**, and treat small-area estimation as a modelling exercise with its own assumptions that slicing further cannot replace.
notes.79: Plot every continuous variable once, unconditionally, before deciding which matter. Exploratory plots have one audience, you, and one requirement: honesty. The table lists what the eye catches that a table hides. **Variables you were not interested in** are where the coding errors live.
notes.80: Small multiples draw many identical small charts in a grid with shared scales. They work for 4–30 panels and fail with auto-scaled panels or 200 panels. **Order panels by something** such as the median or outcome, since ordering is free and does much of the analytical work.
notes.81: Faceting generates small multiples from your data, one panel per category. It is the fastest way to disaggregate visually and catch a Simpson's-paradox reversal. Watch the sample size per panel: **a 10,000-household survey faceted by district** leaves most panels with too few cases to show anything but noise.
notes.82: A box plot shows centre, spread and outliers across groups at a glance, but hides bimodality and the number of observations. Two different shapes can produce identical boxes, so overlay points or use a violin plot where shape matters. **Print the group n under each box.**
notes.83: Same data, two axes. Truncating the y-axis at 90 makes a 4-point rise look like a leap, so bar charts should start at zero. The charts are illustrative. **Check the baseline of every bar chart** you make, including exploratory ones, because a misleading axis fools its author first.
notes.84: Large surveys overplot into a black cloud that hides density. Fix it with transparency, smaller points, sampling, binning or contours, accepting that each trades density information against outlier information. **Often two plots are the honest answer.** With weights, point density misleads: weight the binning or label the plot unweighted.
notes.85: Run this checklist on exploratory plots too. It covers chart type, honest baseline, labelled axes with units, a log scale for money, weighting, disaggregation and stated n. **Put 'unweighted sample' in the subtitle** of unweighted charts, since subtitles travel with screenshots and methods notes do not.
notes.87: EDA ends where testing begins. A pattern found by exploring is a hypothesis, and the clean way to test it is to split the data: explore one half, test on the other. If a split is impossible, **say how many comparisons you looked at** before this one was chosen.
notes.88: Phrase EDA conclusions as descriptions: a distribution, a data-quality problem, a weighted group comparison, a relationship worth testing. Every legitimate claim is descriptive or conditional, and **none asserts cause or significance**. Most of what a practitioner needs from a household survey is descriptive, and describing it correctly is the harder half.
notes.89: The cardinal sin is exploring until something looks significant and then reporting it as confirmed. That is p-hacking by another name, and ordinary curiosity can produce it. The defence is procedural: **write down in advance what you will test, log what you looked at, and report the search** alongside the finding.
notes.90: The table shows how the chance of at least one striking result grows with slices tried: about 5% for one, 23% for five, 64% for twenty, 92% for fifty. It is a rough guide that assumes independent tests and no real effect. **Say how much you explored** so readers can discount.
notes.91: Attach five lines to every finding: unit and denominator, whether weighted, level it holds at, data-quality caveats, and explored or tested. **Keep them in the same file that produces the number**, so caveats cannot drift apart from it. A finding without its caveats is a liability.
notes.92: Translate each finding into plain language a decision maker can act on, using the right-hand phrasings in the table. Each carries the same content and is harder to misread. Tukey's line excuses no imprecision: **the question has to be the right one**, and an approximate answer to it is worth more.
notes.93: Use the five lines as a closing check: look before modelling, know unit, codes and universe, ask why a value is missing, weight population numbers, and treat a found pattern as a question. **Try restating each in a sentence about your own dataset.**
notes.95: Pick the tool by its weights support and by what your team can maintain. R with srvyr and Stata with svyset handle design well, Python needs samplics, and spreadsheets do not. **A spreadsheet's failure mode is no record of what changed**, so keep it for quick looks and use a script for estimates.
notes.96: Prefer a documented script from raw extract to result. The table shows reviewers' questions a script answers directly: where a number came from, what was excluded, how to redo it for 2019, why it changed. **Set a seed and record package versions**, both one line, so 're-run it' becomes a real instruction.
notes.97: Treat these five habits as project hygiene: raw extract read-only and dated, cleaning and analysis in separate scripts, versioned file names, a record of source, download date and filters, and the codebook beside the data. **Avoid 'final_FINAL_v3'**; use names with versions and dates.
notes.98: Use the table to match a source to a need. Microdata needs registration, DHS files are free on request with approval, data.gov.in is rarely unit level, and Census gives tables only. **Download the documentation in the same session as the data**, and record the download date and exact file name.
notes.99: Choose Tukey if you want the attitude and your survey's own report if you want the facts about your file. **Read your survey's methodology note first.** The course pairs with Data Literacy, Quantitative Methods and Research Ethics 101 for the next steps.
